extracted.intended_audience: educators, philosophers, and students of the philosophy of education
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and presents standards for evaluating philosophies of education and theories of knowledge, emphasizing practical, social, and methodological criteria for schooling and inquiry. Oriented to how philosophical positions should shape educational aims, methods, and the formation of dispositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophy as the general theory of education
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophy may be defined as the general theory of education; it is the explicit formulation of the problems of forming right mental and moral habitudes in respect to contemporary social life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a theory makes no difference in educational endeavor, it must be artificial. The educational point of view enables one to envisage philosophic problems where acceptance or rejection makes a difference in practice. Philosophy is not an external application of ready-made ideas but an explicit formulation of educational problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical/educative efficacy of philosophy
rubrics_metrics.description: A philosophy must take effect in conduct; public agitation, propaganda, legislative and administrative action are effective in producing change only in the degree in which they are educative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophy's auditing of past experience and program of values must have educational equivalents; otherwise it remains symbolic, dogmatic, or sentimental. Education of youth offers the best field for modifying dispositions; mere propaganda is compromised because it often targets those whose habits are already set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophy should interpret and critique science for social ends
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophy has a double task: criticizing existing aims with respect to the existing state of science and interpreting the results of specialized science in their bearing on future social endeavor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point out values that have become obsolete given new resources, identify sentimental values lacking means of realization, and show how scientific developments bear on social aims. Successful philosophical work requires educational methods to realize its proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education's aim: formation of fundamental dispositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Education is the process of forming fundamental dispositions, intellectual and emotional, toward nature and fellow men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate educational programs by their capacity to form enduring intellectual and moral attitudes rather than by mere transmission of information; schooling should avoid becoming routine empirical affair without a philosophic survey of its place in contemporary life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject dualism; favor continuity between knowing and activity
rubrics_metrics.description: The correct theory of knowing assumes continuity rather than dualisms (e.g., mind/body, theory/practice); knowing is continuous with activity and involves reorganizing activity rather than being isolated from it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dualisms (empirical vs rational, subject/object, activity vs passivity, intellect vs emotion, knowing vs doing) arise from social divisions. The physiological, biological (evolutionary), and experimental developments support viewing knowing as participation in activity—e.g., the carpenter whose successive motor responses shape subsequent stimuli.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate particulars and generals (avoid sensationalism and pure rationalism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Real knowledge requires both the particularizing function of sense (specifying facts) and the generalizing function of reason (discovering connections); neither bare facts nor bare relations alone suffice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Particulars supply material for knowing; generalities provide means to apply past experience to new situations. Educational methods should train students to perceive events in connection with broader experience (reasonableness = openness to connections), not only to amass particulars or abstract laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning as active, not passive reception
rubrics_metrics.description: Learning should be understood as an active, personally conducted affair (knowing as what the individual does in studying) rather than as passive acquisition of a ready-made external body of truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid instructional models that treat knowledge as stored commodities to be withdrawn; favor pedagogies that engage learners in active reorganization of experience. Anti-patterns include rote reception of subject matter without meaningful application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate intellect and emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: The intellect and the emotions should not be treated as wholly separate; depreciation of interest in education (intellect as pure light, emotions as disturbing heat) is misguided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the role of interest and emotion in motivating learning; reliance on extraneous rewards (exams, marks, prizes, punishments) is symptomatic of a system that devalues intrinsic interest yet depends on external inducements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge as dispositional: organized habits enabling intelligent action
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge consists of intellectual resources—habits organized into dispositions that render our action intelligent; only what is organized into our disposition and used to adapt environment and aims is really knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish knowledge from mere habit: habit gives a single fixed method while knowledge allows selection among many habits and adjusts to novelty. Assess whether instruction builds dispositions usable in new, unforeseen contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental method: knowledge must be tested in action
rubrics_metrics.description: The experimental method has two sides: we have no right to call anything knowledge except where activity has produced changes confirming a conception; and thinking is of avail insofar as anticipation based on observation guides successful action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value thinking as a 'trial of ideas'—experiments of thought that produce observable consequences. Anti-patterns include reliance on dogma or authority instead of testing beliefs; examples contrast 'magic' (trial of luck) with scientific experiment (trial of ideas, learning from failures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prospective/reference-to-future utility of knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge is not merely a survey of what has happened; its reference is future or prospective—it furnishes means for understanding and acting upon what is still going on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate knowledge by its capacity to interpret the unknown, foresee probable futures, and guide plans (illustrated by physician using past findings to interpret and act on present cases). If knowledge is cut off from use in giving meaning to the ongoing, it becomes mere aesthetic contemplation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid scholastic/formal discipline divorced from experience
rubrics_metrics.description: The scholastic/formal-discipline method, useful historically, can become a form of knowing with no special connection to any particular subject matter—making distinctions and classifications for their own sake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Educational anti-pattern: training in formal logic or classificatory exercises without objective or experiential grounding. Schools should not become factories for formal discipline that produces no practical or prospective application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Schools should cultivate inquirers, not merely disciples
rubrics_metrics.description: Under present conditions schools often foster discipleship (acceptance of dogma) rather than inquiry; the scholastic method tends to encourage this.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess curricula by whether they encourage independent inquiry and experimental thinking (John Stuart Mill's critique): prefer pedagogies that promote active testing and responsible use of intelligence over passive acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge increases both power of control and experienced meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Two aspects of knowledge's availability: (i) increased power of control (manage or handle indirectly), and (ii) increased experienced significance—knowledge makes experiences meaningful even when practical control fails.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Educational objectives should target both practical competence (control) and cultivation of meaning. A situation responded to capriciously or by routine yields little conscious significance compared to one interpreted via knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counteract social divisions that produce one-sided intelligence
rubrics_metrics.description: Social divisions (rich/poor, ruling/ruled, differing life-experiences) create dualistic philosophies and leave marks on educational systems, producing one-sided forms of knowing (practical empiricism vs detached rationalism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate educational systems by their capacity to bridge class-based separations in experience—promote continuity in knowing that integrates diverse life-experiences rather than institutionalizing segregated purposes and procedures.
